OneUptime calls acme.crypto (createCsr, readCertificateInfo in Common/Server/Utils/Greenlock/Greenlock.ts), which is built on Node's crypto and @peculiar/x509, and acme-client's forge module only generates keys and signs CSRs: nothing here verifies an RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signature with node-forge, which is where the advisory's forged signatures are accepted.

sprintf-js has no fixed release: <= 1.1.3 is affected and 1.1.3 is the latest. Its one remaining path here is tedious 20.3.4, the TDS driver under mssql (every tedious release, the latest included, requires sprintf-js ^1.1.3); typeorm is flagged only through its optional mssql peer, which it loads only for an mssql DataSource (OneUptime's own database is Postgres), and typeorm-extension only through typeorm. mssql runs in SqlServerConnector (Common/Server/Utils/DataSource/Connectors/SqlServerConnector.ts), against a SQL Server a user configures as a data source, so tedious does parse untrusted server responses. sprintf-js reads a precision only from the format string itself (there is no '*' argument) and hands it to toFixed, toExponential and toPrecision only for %e, %f and %g, so the advisory needs a caller that lets its input become the format string. tedious never does: every sprintf call in it passes a literal format string from tedious's own code (%d, %s, %02X, %04X, %08X; no precision and no %e/%f/%g), and what the server sends (type numbers, data lengths) and the connection settings only ever arrive as arguments. The jest-tooling path (babel-plugin-istanbul -> @istanbuljs/load-nyc-config -> js-yaml 3 -> argparse 1) is gone: this project's override moves load-nyc-config to js-yaml 4, which uses argparse 2.
